Thought: I need to analyze each option to determine when vomiting should not be induced in poisoned persons. This is a medical safety question related to chemical poisoning.

Let me evaluate each option:

A. After ingestion of corrosive substances (e.g., acids, alkalis) - Inducing vomiting with corrosive substances would cause the corrosive material to damage the esophagus and throat again on the way up, potentially causing more harm. This is definitely a case where vomiting should not be induced.

B. After ingestion of foaming substances (e.g., detergents or rinsing agents) - Foaming substances can create excessive foam when vomiting is induced, which could lead to aspiration of the foam into the lungs. This is a case where vomiting should not be induced.

C. After ingestion of highly volatile substances (e.g. gasoline, petroleum) - Volatile substances can be aspirated into the lungs during vomiting, causing chemical pneumonitis. This is a case where vomiting should not be induced.

D. In the case of unconscious or convulsing patients - Unconscious patients cannot protect their airway, so inducing vomiting could lead to aspiration. Similarly, convulsing patients cannot control their vomiting, leading to aspiration risks. This is a case where vomiting should not be induced.

Based on my analysis, all of these options describe situations where vomiting should NOT be induced in poisoned persons. Each presents a specific risk that makes inducing vomiting dangerous.
